propositions.text: Two motions for leave to appeal interlocutory order under Patented Medicines Regulations are before this Court.
propositions.quote: Before this Court are two motions for leave to appeal from a Prothonotary’s interlocutory order made under the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations, S.O.R./93-133, as amended.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states two motions for leave to appeal interlocutory order under the Regulations are before it.

propositions.text: Requirement to obtain leave to appeal interlocutory orders under the Regulations is new as of September 2017.
propositions.quote: The requirement to obtain leave to appeal interlocutory orders under the Regulations is new as of September 2017: Regulations, s. 6.11; Regulations Amending the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations, 2017, S.O.R./2017-166.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes the leave to appeal requirement under the Regulations is new since September 2017.

propositions.text: Since 2017, parties have made submissions on grounds or criteria for granting leave to appeal interlocutory orders under the Regulations.
propositions.quote: Since that time, in many motions for leave to appeal under the Regulations, parties have made submissions concerning the grounds or criteria on which leave to appeal should be granted.

propositions.text: In the two motions before the Court, parties have addressed the issue of grounds or criteria for leave to appeal.
propositions.quote: In the two motions before the Court, parties have also addressed this issue.

paragraphs.summary: The Court observes parties have submitted on grounds for leave to appeal, including in the two motions before it.

propositions.text: This Court has never issued reasons settling the jurisprudential point on leave to appeal interlocutory orders under the Regulations.
propositions.quote: This Court has never issued reasons settling this jurisprudential point.

propositions.text: The Court's settled practice is not to give reasons when deciding leave motions, for expedition and judicial economy.
propositions.quote: This is because the settled practice of this Court for reasons of expedition and judicial economy is not to give reasons when deciding leave motions.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states it has never settled the jurisprudential point and usually does not give reasons on leave motions for expedition.

propositions.text: The Court has departed from its practice of not giving reasons in exceptional circumstances, citing Raincoast Conservation Foundation case.
propositions.quote: However, this Court has departed from this practice in circumstances of extreme exceptionality: see, e.g., Raincoast Conservation Foundation v. Canada (Attorney General), 2019 FCA 224.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes it has given reasons in exceptional cases, citing a prior decision.

propositions.text: The Court is exceptionally providing brief reasons on leave motions to provide guidance on the jurisprudential point.
propositions.quote: In order to provide guidance on this jurisprudential point, this Court is exceptionally providing these one-time, brief reasons concerning these leave motions.

propositions.text: These reasons will be filed in 20-A-21 and a copy in 20-A-25.
propositions.quote: These reasons shall be filed in 20-A-21 and a copy in 20-A-25.

paragraphs.summary: The Court will exceptionally provide brief reasons on leave motions and file them in two dockets.

propositions.text: Applicant for leave to appeal interlocutory order must show a fairly arguable case considering the standard of review.
propositions.quote: an applicant for leave to appeal an interlocutory order under the Regulations must show a fairly arguable case taking into account the standard of review.

propositions.text: Applicant must also show the issue raised can directly impact the overall success or failure of the case.
propositions.quote: But the applicant must also show that the issue raised is capable of having a direct impact on the overall success or failure of the case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states applicants must show a fairly arguable case and that the issue can directly impact the case's success or failure.

propositions.text: Normal standard for granting leave to appeal under Rule 352 is a fairly arguable case, supported by case law.
propositions.quote: The normal standard for granting leave to appeal to this Court under Rule 352 is a “fairly arguable case”: see, e.g., Lukács v. Swoop Inc., 2019 FCA 145 at para. 19; Lufthansa German Airlines v. Canadian Transportation Agency, 2005 FCA 295, 346 N.R. 79 at para. 9; Canada (Minister of Human Resources Development) v. Rafuse, 2002 FCA 31, 222 F.T.R. 160 at para. 12; Martin v. Canada (Minister of Human Resources Development) (1999), 252 N.R. 141 (F.C.A.).

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the normal standard for leave to appeal is a fairly arguable case, citing authorities.

propositions.text: Evaluation of fairly arguable case must consider appellate standard of review.
propositions.quote: The evaluation of a “fairly arguable case” must take place bearing in mind the appellate standard of review: in related contexts, see Hébert v. Wenham, 2020 FCA 186 at paras. 11-14 and Raincoast Conservation Foundation v. Canada (Attorney General), 2019 FCA 224 at para. 16.

propositions.text: Applicant must show it can arguably overcome any deferential standard applying in the appeal.
propositions.quote: In particular, the applicant must show that it can arguably overcome any deferential standard that applies in the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the fairly arguable case evaluation must consider the appellate standard and overcoming deferential review.

propositions.text: It is easier to make out a fairly arguable case under correctness review than under palpable and overriding error review.
propositions.quote: a party moving for leave to appeal can make out a fairly arguable case more easily under correctness review than under review for palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: Showing arguable failure of correctness review differs from showing arguable failure of palpable and overriding error review.
propositions.quote: Showing that something arguably fails correctness review—i.e., is arguably wrong—is one thing. Showing that something arguably fails review for palpable and overriding error—i.e., the arguable presence of one or more obvious errors which individually or collectively may affect the outcome of the matter—is quite another.

propositions.text: Cites Housen, Hospira, Mahjoub cases on standard of review distinctions.
propositions.quote: See Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235; Hospira Healthcare Corporation v. Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, 2016 FCA 215, [2017] 1 F.C.R. 331; Mahjoub v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FCA 157, [2018] 2 F.C.R. 344 at paras. 58-74.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the difference between correctness and palpable error standards with case citations.

propositions.text: Considerable deference to case management orders increases the burden on applicants for leave to appeal.
propositions.quote: The considerable deference this Court gives to case management orders adds to the burden the applicant for leave to appeal must surmount.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes deference to case management orders increases the applicant's burden for leave.

propositions.text: Court must scrutinize alleged errors to distinguish legal errors from factually suffused matters requiring palpable and overriding error standard.
propositions.quote: The Court must scrutinize the alleged error to see if it is, despite what counsel says, a factually suffused matter that can be set aside only for palpable and overriding error: Canada (National Revenue) v. JP Morgan Asset Management (Canada) Inc., 2013 FCA 250, [2014] 2 F.C.R. 557 at paras. 49-50.

propositions.text: Counsel often characterize factual matters as legal errors, but Court must assess properly.
propositions.quote: good counsel, in pursuing the interests of their clients, tend to characterize something as an error of law or of extricable principle when, in fact, it is nothing of the sort.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains it must distinguish true legal errors from factual matters despite counsel's characterizations.

propositions.text: Fairly arguable case is usual standard for leave to appeal, meaning leave should not be granted if appeal unlikely to succeed.
propositions.quote: A fairly arguable case is the usual and default standard for motions for leave to appeal. This merely confirms that there is no sense granting leave to an appeal that is very unlikely to succeed.

propositions.text: Sometimes legislation requires more than arguability for leave to appeal, as in Raincoast case.
propositions.quote: But sometimes legislation providing for motions for leave to appeal requires the applicant for leave to show more: e.g., Raincoast at paras. 9-16.

propositions.text: To determine if more is required, interpret legislation in light of text, context and purpose, citing Rizzo and Bell ExpressVu.
propositions.quote: To find out whether this is so, we must interpret the legislation in light of its text, context and purpose: see, e.g., Re Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 27, 154 D.L.R. (4th) 193 and Bell ExpressVu Limited Partnership v. Rex, 2002 SCC 42, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 559.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states fairly arguable case is usual standard but legislation may require more, requiring interpretation of text, context and purpose.

propositions.text: Regulations require applicant to show more than arguability due to 2017 amendments aimed at expedition and preventing unnecessary appeals.
propositions.quote: we conclude that the Regulations require an applicant to show more than just arguability. The 2017 amendments to the Regulations were aimed at expedition and preventing unnecessary appeals.

propositions.text: 2017 amendments removed interlocutory appeals as of right and allowed appeals directly to this Court, suggesting only significant interlocutory matters get leave and quickly.
propositions.quote: They removed the ability of a party to appeal interlocutory decisions as of right. They also permitted appeals to go directly to this Court, bypassing one level of court. These suggest that only interlocutory matters of prime significance and materiality should be given leave and, even then, they must be dealt with quickly.

propositions.text: Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement confirms the purpose of amendments.
propositions.quote: The Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement confirms and underscores this: see Canada Gazette Part II, v. 151, Extra No. 1 (September 7, 2017) at 34.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes the Regulations require more than arguability due to 2017 amendments aimed at expedition and significance, confirmed by Regulatory Impact Analysis.

propositions.text: Applicant must persuade Court that interlocutory appeal decision will directly impact overall success or failure of the case.
propositions.quote: Thus, an applicant for leave to appeal must also persuade the Court that its decision on the interlocutory appeal will have a direct impact on the overall success or failure of the case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states applicants must show the interlocutory appeal will directly impact the case's success or failure.

propositions.text: Leave should be denied if interlocutory order upholds refusal to answer questions and answers won't impact case success or failure.
propositions.quote: leave should be denied where the Prothonotary has upheld a party’s refusal to answer questions and the answers to the questions will not have a direct impact on the success or failure of the case.

propositions.text: This is especially so if Prothonotary assessed proportionality or relationship of questions to case issues, a factually suffused assessment deserving deference.
propositions.quote: This is all the more so where, either as part of an assessment of proportionality or otherwise, the Prothonotary has commented on the relationship between a question and the issues that the case will turn upon. This is usually a factually suffused assessment calling for deference.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains leave should be denied if refusal to answer questions won't impact case, especially if Prothonotary assessed proportionality.

propositions.text: Both motions fail the test for leave; neither is fairly arguable given appellate standard of review.
propositions.quote: both motions fail to satisfy the test for leave. Both are not fairly arguable, particularly given the appellate standard of review.

propositions.text: One motion involves factual and discretionary application of Rule 249; the other is a straightforward discretionary discovery issue.
propositions.quote: One is an orthodox, factual and discretionary application of Rule 249 while the other is a straight-forward, discretionary discovery issue.

propositions.text: Neither motion involves an issue of law or extricable legal principle.
propositions.quote: Looking at the true character of the alleged errors, the Court concludes that neither involves an issue of law or extricable legal principle.

propositions.text: If leave were granted, decision would not directly impact overall success or failure of the cases.
propositions.quote: This Court is satisfied that if leave were granted, its decision would not have a direct impact on the overall success or failure of the cases.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds both motions fail the leave test, involve no legal issues, and would not impact case outcomes.

propositions.text: The Court will dismiss the leave motions with costs.
propositions.quote: Therefore, we will dismiss the leave motions with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The Court dismisses the leave motions with costs.
